strengths: The paper addresses an important question: why adversarially trained models can generalize on clean inputs while retaining a large robust generalization gap. Studying representation complexity alongside training dynamics is a useful approach.
The signal/noise decomposition makes the proposed mechanism interpretable and provides measurable quantities for studying feature learning and memorization.
The empirical investigation includes synthetic data, MNIST, and CIFAR10, reports clean and robust performance separately, and provides additional diagnostics of input-loss flatness.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.4 is false under its stated assumptions. Consider a balanced distribution on (±e1, ±1), radius δ = 1/4, and clean classifier f(x) = x1 + 7/8. This satisfies Assumptions 4.1–4.3. As the sample size grows, both atoms have empirical mass near 1/2, so o(1) robust training error forces zero robust test error, excluding CGRO. The assumptions need restrictions on population mass covered by training neighborhoods. Furthermore, Assumption 4.2 separates opposite classes; it does not imply the pairwise disjoint training balls used in Lemma 4.5.

The representation proof has an additional approximation gap. Appendix F claims uniform o(1) approximation of the generally discontinuous indicator-based construction by continuous ReLU networks. Such approximation is impossible across a nonvanishing jump. Introducing soft indicators requires a different argument controlling transition regions and classification margins; the proof supplies neither.

Theorem 5.9 does not establish robustness under the threat model in Definition 3.4. Training attacks modify only the signal patch along w*, whereas CGRO requires low training error against the full perturbation ball. This discrepancy is substantive: under the stated scaling, total noise norm is o(α) and δ approaches α. A full ℓ2 adversary can reverse the noise patches while shrinking the signal to o(α), producing negative training margins at the claimed U = Θ(α^−q), V_i = Θ(1) solution.

The dynamics and generalization proofs contain further invalid steps. Appendix E.12 treats cubic Gaussian noise as sub-Gaussian and uses a concentration expression that does not account for dependence across neurons sharing the same test patch. Cubic Gaussian variables are not generally sub-Gaussian. The signal-growth argument also drops the factor 1−λ even though Assumption 5.7 permits λ = 1. These errors affect the claimed learning phases and test-error guarantees.

The experiments do not adequately validate the theoretical explanation. Section 6.2 sets δ = α = 10, violating the required δ < α and permitting complete removal of the stated informative signal. Poor robust performance therefore does not isolate the proposed learning mechanism. In Table 1, the CIFAR10 robust gap increases overall from 20.80 to 49.49 percentage points, with only a small late decrease. Chance-level training performance of smaller MNIST models also cannot distinguish representation limitations from optimization failure. Missing PGD step counts, step sizes, restarts, optimizer schedules, and variability across runs limit reproducibility and confidence in the robustness measurements.

The additional generalization bound in Theorem B.1 is unsupported as stated. A constant nonzero predictor has zero input-loss gradient but label-dependent losses, so its population and empirical risks still fluctuate with sampled class proportions. The proposed bound would require population risk to be no larger than empirical risk with high probability, without any sampling-error term. Appendix G also retains bandwidth- and confidence-dependent terms that are not justified away in the theorem.

The originality and scope of the lower-bound contribution need clearer justification. Theorem 4.7 is existential over a distribution class that already includes the linearly separable examples considered by Li et al. (2022), and Appendix F again constructs linearly separable data. This does not establish a stronger lower bound. A worst-case existence result also cannot substantiate the broadly presented capacity hierarchy for practical datasets. The potentially useful combined perspective requires sound central results before its significance can be assessed favorably.
